The community had to distinguish tasks previously united in one life: governing, preserving recitation and reports, issuing judgments and learning how to act. Different arrangements for those tasks became major features of subsequent Islamic civilization.
chapters.sharh:
The pilgrimage's actions are preserved through differing Companions, notably the extended report of Jābir in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, Book of Pilgrimage, no. 1218 in common numbering. Qurʾān 5:3 is linked in the received tradition to the completion of religion, while legal details arise through multiple reports and juristic comparisons. Versions of the Farewell Sermon differ in wording, while repeatedly addressing the sanctity of life and property, inherited abuses and obligations between members of the community. The historical significance of embodied instruction is strong: when an act is publicly demonstrated before witnesses, its later transmission can draw upon what people saw as well as what they heard. But witnesses differ in attention and memory, explaining why later scholars examined reports and reconciled apparent discrepancies.

The later multiplication of disciplines is easier to understand if we first separate the questions. What did the Prophet teach or do? Who witnessed it? Which of those actions binds others, and under what conditions? Who has authority to judge a dispute now? What dispositions make the instruction inwardly fruitful? Hadith criticism addresses the reliability of transmission; jurisprudence its normative application; political theory the government of the community; spiritual instruction its realization in character. In the Prophet's lifetime these functions met in a single authoritative person, though many companions already served as teachers or agents. His death therefore did not create knowledge out of nothing, but changed how different kinds of authority were accessed and coordinated.

The Prophet's death made an analytical distinction unavoidable. His authority included receiving revelation, teaching its meaning, judging disputes, leading worship and directing communal affairs. The end of prophecy did not end any of the community's practical needs, yet the functions could not all be inherited in the same manner. Sunni accounts emphasize the formation of the caliphate and the wider transmission of knowledge by the Companions; Imāmī accounts place particular interpretive authority in the divinely designated Imams. Sunni and Shiʿi accounts of the Prophet's final instructions later informed distinct understandings of political leadership and religious authority. Al-Ghazālī, Shādhilī authors and Akbarian thinkers later explored prophetic inheritance as the formation of character or realization of spiritual wisdom. These are serious retrospective interpretations, not evidence that the first assembly at Saqīfah already used their technical distinctions. The demands of leadership and expansion made these distinctions urgent long before jurists and spiritual authors gave them their later technical forms.

The Farewell Pilgrimage provides a public model of worship, but a great deal of the Sunnah reached later generations through domestic life and instruction outside large gatherings. Reports through ʿĀʾishah, Umm Salamah and others matter particularly for private conduct and interpretation of what the Prophet intended. Later scholars' distinctions between common practice, judicial rulings and prophetic particularities are analytical responses to the differing settings of those reports; they are not a ready-made classification uttered at the final pilgrimage.

The later question of succession arises because different functions performed by the Prophet could be transmitted in different ways without implying that revelation continued. A transmitted report could preserve his practice; a judge could apply it; a teacher could cultivate virtues exemplified in it; political leadership required a decision about public allegiance and coercive power. The Sunni and Shiʿi discussions of rightful leadership should be set at the relevant early chapters without equating them with the entire history of spiritual inheritance. Later technical accounts of *walāyah* must be traced through their own authors and texts (Dossier 7).

chapters.title: After the Prophet: allegiance and the survival of obligations
chapters.book: Book IV — Succession, conquest and imperial government
chapters.matn: After the Prophet's death the Anṣār met at the Saqīfah of Banū Sāʿidah to consider leadership; Abū Bakr and other leading emigrants joined the discussion, and he received allegiance, followed by broader acceptance. The Prophet's family had not taken part in the initial meeting, and disagreement over leadership and certain property claims remained. Meanwhile, some Arabian groups questioned obligations that had bound them to Madinah, disputed zakāt payments or followed rival claimants to prophecy. Abū Bakr insisted that the public obligations established during the Prophet's life were not dissolved by his death. The campaigns of the Ridda, including the fighting against Musaylimah at al-Yamāmah, restored control over much of Arabia at considerable cost. The same period stimulated concern for preserving the recited text and for maintaining officials and commanders across distant communities. Abū Bakr's caliphate lasted only two years, but it settled an immediate question of government in practice: a common religious life would require leadership capable of acting after the Messenger's death. It did not settle every later theological question about who possessed rightful interpretive and spiritual authority.
chapters.sharh:
The surviving accounts identify disputes over allegiance, consultation, the Prophet's family and the authority of the first caliph. Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, reports concerning the allegiance and ʿUmar's retrospective description of Saqīfah, and the traditions concerning Fāṭimah's claim and ʿAlī's later allegiance are essential Sunni witnesses. They require direct reading, not paraphrases that erase conflict. Sunni theology generally distinguishes the non-prophetic office of caliph from the Prophetic gift of revelation; Twelver Shiʿi theology argues that ʿAlī and the Imams possess a divinely designated leadership and authoritative religious guidance. Ghadīr Khumm and the relation of *mawlā* to *wilāyah* feature in the dispute, but a full evaluation of competing reports would displace the history's principal purpose. Sunni discussions generally ground Abū Bakr's caliphate in allegiance and communal obligation; Twelver Shiʿi discussions understand ʿAlī's authority through the doctrine of designation and the Imam's religious office.

The difficulty of succession was especially acute because the Prophet left several kinds of obligation in operation. A governor needed orders, a tax collector needed authorization, an army needed command, and a family needed to know whom to consult over a dispute. The early pledge to Abū Bakr addressed the public coordination of those tasks. It did not remove affection and distinct religious claims attached to the Prophet's household. Keeping these forms of concern separate clarifies both the practical necessity Sunni sources emphasize and the continuing Imāmī argument about divinely designated guidance. Conquests subsequently multiplied the need for commanders, governors, judges and officials able to administer distant provinces.

Abū Bakr's insistence on continued zakāt payments was a decision about whether public obligations survived the Prophet's death. It should not be confused with the distinct theological question of authoritative succession. The Sunni account treats his caliphate as the first political continuation; Twelver Shiʿi doctrine gives ʿAlī a divinely designated place in the succession to religious guidance. Only the indispensable evidence and principal interpretive difference belong here; the disputed speeches and details of Fadak can remain in a focused note.

The Ridda involved more than a uniform attempt to renounce religion. The actions of different tribes concerned tax, allegiance, local autonomy and prophetic claimants in varying combinations. Keeping military and fiscal relationships functioning was crucial to sustaining the new association: without it, local commanders, teachers and communities would operate under incompatible claims of authority. The concern for collection of Qurʾānic material after al-Yamāmah is narrated in Bukhārī and later compilations; the surviving accounts should be handled as traditions about preservation, not as proof that no writing existed before 632. The expansion after Abū Bakr built on this reconsolidation but exposed the community to institutions much larger than those of Arabia.

chapters.title: Conquest and the problems inherited from older empires
chapters.book: Book IV — Succession, conquest and imperial government
chapters.matn: Abū Bakr had struggled to maintain the obligations of communities already associated with Madinah. Under ʿUmar, armies moving beyond Arabia confronted the established powers of Syria, Iraq and Egypt. The battles at al-Yarmūk and al-Qādisiyyah brought military victory, but governing the conquered lands demanded skills unlike those needed to win them. Towns still required grain; fields still needed irrigation; churches, monasteries and village communities had their own leadership; tax officials understood accounts in Greek, Coptic or Persian. Soldiers expected payment and the people who remained on the land expected to cultivate it. The new rulers could not make all these arrangements anew. They negotiated submissions, retained many local officials and gathered revenue through modified versions of older systems. Garrison settlements, especially al-Baṣrah, al-Kūfah and al-Fusṭāṭ, kept substantial bodies of troops together without dispersing them among every village. Victory thus brought the Muslims into daily responsibility for populations whose religious affiliations, languages and economic practices had not changed with their governors. These responsibilities created the setting in which later debates about land, taxation, public justice and the rights of non-Muslim communities became unavoidable.
chapters.sharh:
Conquest gave commanders territory, but administering that territory required decisions about cultivators, local officials, soldiers and revenue. Armies could acquire territorial authority in a campaigning season; provisioning troops and assessing land required continuing negotiation with cultivators, notables and former officials. Al-Balādhurī's *Futūḥ al-buldān* preserves accounts of treaties and settlements, but details vary across recensions and may reflect subsequent fiscal controversies. Administrative papyri and coins offer independent controls on gradual changes in government and language. Muslim governors adapted some existing fiscal practices and altered others; the conquered provinces did not immediately share one uniform tax code. The Syrian, Iraqi and Egyptian arrangements followed different trajectories.

The division between garrison and countryside helps explain why the conquerors' language and legal practices could spread without immediately making the subject population Muslim. Tax resources went to military stipends and government, while established cultivators and religious institutions continued many activities. The eventual change of language, conversion and local custom therefore took generations and differed by region. This is where the question of just administration began to be pursued beyond personal adjudication in Madinah: the ruler had to decide how much to levy, who possessed land, which agreements were binding and how to restrain troops. The moral language of justice was inherited from the Prophetic teaching, but its application now involved a more complex set of agents and documents. Hugh Kennedy and the *New Cambridge History of Islam* document the variation among conquest settlements; surviving treaty reports do not preserve one uniform agreement.

Dated receipts and correspondence from Egypt preserve administrative practices that continued or changed under Muslim rule. A landholder and a soldier encountered power differently: the soldier needed regular provisions; the cultivator needed a predictable demand and protection from arbitrary seizure. Their interaction connected military policy to harvest cycles and irrigation. Nor is the word *jizyah* consistently used for one identical early fiscal arrangement in all sources; terminology and practice need local comparison. This matters to the later juristic tradition because arguments about the rights of cultivators and protected communities emerged in the aftermath of real negotiated settlements, some remembered through legalizing retrospective narratives. After victory, officials collected revenue, cultivators worked the land, and commanders supplied troops; these recurring duties sustained political control beyond the battlefield.

chapters.title: The garrison, the treasury and the provincial community
chapters.book: Book IV — Succession, conquest and imperial government
chapters.matn: In the new garrison towns, soldiers lived with their families, received stipends and gradually made places for merchants, freed persons, jurists and teachers. Their quarters often followed tribal affiliations; common prayer and military command therefore existed beside familiar bonds of kin and patronage. ʿUmar's registers of payment recognized differences of service and standing, and the distribution of revenue required information about households, campaigns and rights of recipients. In Iraq, keeping extensive cultivated land under continuing taxation, rather than dividing it all permanently among victorious soldiers, sustained payments beyond a single generation. Arab tribal groups had become provincial communities, but the money that sustained them came increasingly from settled agricultural populations. At the same time, new Muslims entered these communities through conversion, marriage, alliance and clientage. Their claims to social equality and fiscal treatment did not always fit the privileges of the earliest military settlers. The government's efforts to maintain cohesion created problems that accompanied the Umayyad period: who counted as a member of the ruling community, how service was rewarded, and whether the treasury belonged to an army, a dynasty or the wider body of believers.
chapters.sharh:
The *dīwān* was a register and payment system, not the equivalent of a modern civil service or a census of all residents. Reports about its foundation and the hierarchy of stipends must be compared with later practice. Fred Donner traces the interaction of military recruitment, settlement and revenue administration during the early Islamic conquests. The precise policy on Iraqi land is known partly through retrospective juristic accounts in which allocation of conquered lands had become a legal problem.

This is an appropriate place for Ibn Khaldūn as a later interpreter: solidarity can gather and defend a military group, while durable rule depends on the ability to administer territories and revenues wider than the original solidarities. Yet he cannot substitute for the details of seventh-century stipends and provinces. A converted Persian client in al-Kūfah, a landed Christian family in Syria and an Arab soldier receiving payments did not enter the same arrangement. Soldiers, cultivators, clients, officials and scholars held different claims on revenues, property and public authority. It also explains why towns of conquest became centres of learning: they housed people who needed judgments on marriage, sale, slavery, inheritance and disputes involving communities with different practices. Students learned from Companions and successors amid these recurring problems rather than in a social vacuum.

Differences in military stipends shaped household income, prestige and competition for public resources. If an early participant in the campaigns held a recognised claim on the treasury, a later convert or client might not possess an equivalent claim even when sharing the same worship. That tension helps explain debates about the *mawālī* and the eventual pressures on Umayyad government. It should not be asserted that every client was excluded or every province followed one discriminatory rule. Some were wealthy and influential, and recruitment and fiscal practice changed. The closer historical explanation follows a particular garrison's register, its sources of revenue and its social composition. The relation between inherited solidarity and religious universalism becomes visible through conflicts over payment and status. It also clarifies why instruction mattered: a growing town needed means to identify valid testimony, settle competing property claims and teach new residents obligations that had developed first among a much smaller community.

chapters.title: Civil war and the limits of loyalty
chapters.book: Book IV — Succession, conquest and imperial government
chapters.matn: Expansion increased the powers of provincial commanders and the resources at stake in their appointments. Complaints against ʿUthmān's government sharpened until rebels killed him in Madinah in 656. ʿAlī received allegiance while others demanded that the murderers first be punished; in the disorder no agreement existed about who could enforce that punishment or command the armies needed to do so. Fighting followed near al-Baṣrah and later at Ṣiffīn against Muʿāwiyah's Syrian forces. Arbitration, proposed to halt the conflict, divided ʿAlī's supporters and led to further violence with the Khārijites. ʿAlī was killed in 661. Al-Ḥasan then made a settlement with Muʿāwiyah, bringing an end to that phase of warfare. Supporters divided over allegiance to a caliph, responsibility for ʿUthmān's killing, obedience to commanders and the Prophet's family's claims to leadership. Those disputes survived the immediate fighting and later shaped accounts of legitimate authority, grave sin and rebellion.
chapters.sharh:
The broad order of events is well attested in early Muslim historiography; the words attributed to individual participants, precise motives and details of arbitration require more caution. Al-Ṭabarī brings together reports from transmitters with different affiliations, and these are not independent eyewitness accounts merely because they appear side by side. Sunni histories recognize the leading Companions' standing while preserving accounts of disputed decisions, armed conflict and deaths among their supporters. Shiʿi accounts give the rights and designation of ʿAlī a different constitutional and theological meaning. Sunni and Shiʿi arguments about legitimate authority developed amid disputes over retaliation, military allegiance and the duties of government.

The civil war also had geographical and material mechanisms. The garrison army of Iraq and the Syrian command were organized forces with their own leadership, pay and attachments. Muʿāwiyah could rely upon a developed provincial military apparatus; ʿAlī had to govern amid divided coalitions and disputes about the killing of ʿUthmān. Later kalām arguments about a grave sinner and political obedience grew in a world that remembered those choices. Rival factions invoked justice, but disputed who possessed authority to punish ʿUthmān's killers and whether political allegiance must precede retaliation. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Balādhurī preserve differing accounts of the first fitna, especially in reported speeches and motives; their transmissions do not independently establish each participant's private intentions.

Later theological classifications of the first fitna do not establish the exact beliefs or motives of every participant in the original conflicts. The battle at Ṣiffīn and the division over arbitration help explain how political disagreement prompted debates over the relation between judgment and divine law. The outcomes of the battles do not establish that every participant held the fully developed doctrines later associated with Khārijites, Sunnis or Shiʿa. The extant speeches are transmitted through literary and partisan filters. The strongest causal account connects the troops' alliances, demands about the killing of ʿUthmān and the procedural problem of retaliation. The later theological writings can then be read as responses to the remembered crisis, with their own dates and purposes. The disputes over allegiance, retaliation and ʿAlī's authority shaped later Sunni and Shiʿi understandings of legitimate government.

chapters.title: Damascus, Karbalāʾ and the making of an imperial administration
chapters.book: Book IV — Succession, conquest and imperial government
chapters.matn: Muʿāwiyah ruled from Damascus with Syrian military support and an administration able to draw on older provincial practices. His nomination of Yazīd placed hereditary succession at the centre of a dispute that the settlement with al-Ḥasan had not finally resolved. Al-Ḥusayn refused allegiance, travelled toward Kūfah after appeals from supporters, and was killed with members of his family and companions at Karbalāʾ in 680. The event gave the claims of the Prophet's household an enduring place in Muslim religious memory. Civil war continued until ʿAbd al-Malik consolidated authority. Under him and his successors, the state issued new coinage, enlarged the role of Arabic in administration and invested in prominent buildings, including the Dome of the Rock. Governors and armies extended authority toward the Iberian Peninsula, Central Asia and Sind. The resulting empire was increasingly visible as a single political order, but its provinces differed in language, law and social composition. The government could regulate revenue and command troops more readily than it could determine what every believer should accept as authoritative religious teaching.
chapters.sharh:
Al-Ḥusayn and his companions were killed at Karbalāʾ; reports of speeches and exact casualty figures vary among later transmitters. The death of al-Ḥusayn and his companions is foundational to Shiʿi historical memory, while Sunni accounts also affirm the wrong and grief of the event, even as theological readings diverge. Al-Ṭabarī's use of Abū Mikhnaf and later treatments by al-Mufīd overlap in transmission; agreement between them cannot automatically be counted as independent attestation.

Umayyad coins, inscriptions and buildings record official policies and dynastic claims that later chronicles recount through their own traditions. Currency reform mattered because weights, taxes and payments connected distant provinces through common state symbols and procedures. Arabic administrative change was uneven, and the presence of Arabic in registers did not immediately displace Greek, Coptic and Persian from society. Nor should political consolidation be equated with universal religious acceptance. Schools of Qurʾānic recitation, ascetic teaching and early legal discussion grew within and sometimes against the horizons of state power. Al-Ḥajjāj's governorship and the experience of Iraqi opposition also reveal coercive dimensions of the imperial project. The distinction between the caliph's political authority and a teacher's credibility becomes more intelligible through these particular institutional pressures.

The Dome of the Rock supplies a particularly revealing contrast between official and social evidence. Its Arabic inscriptions present theological claims in a public imperial setting; its construction dates and physical form can be investigated independently of late court anecdotes. Coin inscriptions and administrative documents trace changes in how the state represented and financed itself. Yet none of these tells us what every market trader believed or how every household taught the Qurʾān. That difference matters: an empire may adopt common public signs while local traditions continue in distinct languages and social groups. In later decades the *mawālī*, tax burdens and provincial grievances entered contests over rule. The Abbasid movement arose within a consolidated Umayyad empire where political stability had not settled competing claims to leadership and status.

chapters.title: The Abbasid revolution and a change of ruling centre
chapters.book: Book IV — Succession, conquest and imperial government
chapters.matn: By the middle of the eighth century, the Umayyad empire possessed formidable fiscal and military resources but faced opposition among groups dissatisfied with provincial rule, status and the distribution of authority. In Khurāsān, networks of Arab settlers and others were mobilized in a movement promising rule associated with the Prophet's family. Under Abū Muslim's command, its armies advanced west and defeated the Umayyads in 750. The Abbasids became caliphs, and the centre of government moved toward Iraq. The revolution did not redistribute authority equally among its supporters: the new rulers built a dynasty with its own claims, commanders and administrators, while ʿAlid expectations persisted. Al-Manṣūr chose a new site on the Tigris for Baghdad, bringing the court closer to Iraqi agricultural revenues, eastern communication routes and the skills of Persianate secretarial households. What had begun as a contest over legitimate rule became the foundation of a metropolis where political power, commerce and scholarship would meet. The earlier garrison cities remained significant, but the new capital drew specialists from several regions and languages into a shared urban economy.
chapters.sharh:
The Abbasid movement recruited support across several groups, including Khurāsānian military and political networks, and did not represent only non-Arab converts. The movement involved overlapping interests in Khurāsān, including established Arab settler communities, patron-client networks, religious expectations and military organization. Its slogans did not prescribe a single later theory of authority. Consult al-Ṭabarī alongside studies of the Abbasid revolution by M. A. Shaban and Elton Daniel, while recognizing disagreements in their reconstructions.

Khurāsānian support and the establishment of Baghdad in Iraq shifted the caliphate's military and administrative centre eastward. Iraq sat near productive agricultural districts and routes connecting Iran, the Gulf and Syria; Baghdad's foundation under al-Manṣūr in 762 deliberately concentrated administration. But courts do not create intellectual life by decree. The city inherited teachers, translators and merchants from older centres, while paper, libraries, private patrons and students increasingly made scholarship possible beyond the immediate court. Baghdad's scholarly activity depended on administrators, merchants, patrons, booksellers, translators and teachers, not on its foundation alone. Dynastic legitimacy, in turn, continued to be debated among jurists, Alids and different provincial populations; the Abbasid revolution settled who ruled, not every question of who could teach or interpret revelation.

chapters.title: Baghdad and the work of a learned city
chapters.book: Book V — How knowledge and spiritual formation acquired lasting institutions
chapters.matn: Baghdad drew court officials, traders, physicians, craftsmen and students to a place where goods and ideas arrived by river, road and caravan. The treasury paid armies and officials, but private households and patrons also supported books, teachers and specialized work. Physicians inherited Greek and Syriac medical learning and adapted it to new patients and institutions; mathematicians and astronomers addressed problems arising from calculation, observation and earlier sciences. Translators could work across Syriac, Greek and Arabic, while jurists and transmitters met learners who came to study accounts of the Prophet and their implications. Paper and book markets made it easier to reproduce, annotate and circulate substantial texts. Yet the city's different enquiries did not form one institution: some occurred in courts, others in mosques, private houses, bookshops or medical circles. The caliphs could sponsor scholars and also coerce them. As the city expanded, its intellectual authority depended increasingly on the quality of transmission and argument within communities of learning as well as the favour of those who ruled it.
chapters.sharh:
Hārūn al-Rashīd's court and al-Maʾmūn's patronage are important, but the familiar story of a single 'House of Wisdom' producing all the sciences suppresses the multiplicity of patrons and workplaces. Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq's translation projects, al-Kindī's philosophical circle and the mathematical writing associated with al-Khwārizmī had distinct aims and constituencies. Dimitri Gutas, *Greek Thought, Arabic Culture*, and research on medicine and translation distinguish court translation from wider patterns of scholarly patronage. The adoption of paper expanded the possibilities for copying without making manuscripts cheap for every reader.

Baghdad gathered translators, booksellers, physicians, administrators and patrons who sustained scholarly work through different institutions. Secretarial administration required numeracy and records; medicine attracted patrons and clinical expertise; juridical differences demanded teachers able to transmit and reason; rich households could sustain independent specialists. This is the sort of joint historical explanation Hodgson was seeking when he discussed the interaction of state, merchant and learned interests. But the learned world was not always harmoniously plural. In the *miḥnah*, caliphal demands about the createdness of the Qurʾān brought public theology and state coercion together. Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal's refusal and later memory of the episode exemplify a struggle over the boundary between the ruler's command and a scholar's religious authority. It would be misleading either to call this a conflict between 'religion' and 'science' or to identify all speculative inquiry with official coercion.

The history of translation is most persuasive when treated through a defined task. Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq's work on Greek medical texts involved comparing copies, choosing technical equivalents and revising earlier translations; a practitioner then had to interpret the resulting Arabic work in relation to patients and other medical knowledge. The procedure differed from al-Khwārizmī's mathematical writing or a jurist's evaluation of a report, even when they shared bookshops and patrons. For this reason 'Islamic science' is a historical umbrella, not the name of one single method. During the *miḥnah*, caliphal authorities sponsored intellectual inquiry while pressuring scholars to affirm a particular doctrine about the Qurʾān. Intellectual life became durable through a plurality of communities capable of criticising, transmitting and sponsoring knowledge, although their relative independence varied. Individual translations passed through named patrons, scribes, translators and readers, often with several stages of revision.

chapters.title: Travelers, households and the authentication of transmitted learning
chapters.book: Book V — How knowledge and spiritual formation acquired lasting institutions
chapters.matn: A student wishing to learn the Prophet's teaching could begin with a parent or a local teacher, but difficult reports often sent students to other towns. They asked who had heard a narration, compared its wording, and learned how particular authorities prayed, judged or answered questions. The journeys formed a network in which Madinah, Makkah, Kūfah, Baṣrah, Damascus, Egypt and later Khurāsān were connected by repeated encounters. Teachers sometimes disagreed because they possessed different reports or understood an action's circumstances differently. As traditions multiplied, scholars recorded transmitters' lives and examined interruptions, discrepancies and defects in chains and texts. The collections associated with al-Bukhārī and Muslim emerged within this world of travel, questioning and written compilation. Women as well as men preserved and taught reports, beginning prominently with members of the Prophet's household and continuing through later scholarly families. These practices made religious memory portable, yet they also demanded a discipline of verification: a report's presence in a book did not alone determine what it meant or how it should be applied.
chapters.sharh:
The *isnād* was an explicit claim about routes of transmission, not a mechanical guarantee of truth. Some students transmitted from personal audition, some from reading or authorization, and scholars debated these methods. Differences among *ṣaḥīḥ*, *ḥasan*, *ḍaʿīf* and other classifications developed through particular critical conventions; the two canonical Ṣaḥīḥs were not produced under one uniform ancient state procedure. The introductory material in Muslim's *Ṣaḥīḥ*, al-Bukhārī's chapter headings and later discussions by Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ help explain the criteria. The historical date of a report and a ḥadīth critic's judgment of its acceptability answer separate questions. Harald Motzki compares chains and wording to reconstruct stages of transmission; scholars contest some of the conclusions drawn from those comparisons.

The household was not marginal to this process. ʿĀʾishah was asked about private worship, domestic conduct and the circumstances of legal pronouncements because these subjects often lay outside male public observation. Later women transmitters and teachers, documented in biographical dictionaries, were associated with scholarly households and institutions, although participation varied by region and century. Households, mosques and traveling students preserved Prophetic practice across cities without relying on a single caliphal archive. Traveling students and scholarly correspondence gradually connected distant communities while leaving room for local practices and disagreements.

Report critics compared transmissions from different cities to identify common wording, variations and possible shared sources. If two students in different cities transmitted what they said was the same Prophetic report, the critic might compare the named links in their chains, the wording of the two texts and reports about the reliability and contact of the transmitters. Agreement might reflect shared earlier transmission rather than independent corroboration; difference might arise from abbreviation, memory or a genuine alternate wording. Inclusion in a collection did not settle a report's wording, original setting or legal application. A jurist might accept a report's transmission yet debate whether an action was obligatory, recommended or context-specific. Jurists then assessed whether reliable reports established obligation, recommendation, permission or a ruling specific to one occasion. Women such as ʿĀʾishah transmitted knowledge through identifiable households and teaching relationships; their roles and opportunities varied among regions and generations.

Transmission became accountable precisely because different students could preserve different wordings or levels of detail. A particularly strong example comes from the *Muwaṭṭaʾ*: El Shamsy compares the recensions of Yaḥyā al-Laythī, Abū Muṣʿab and Ibn Bukayr with quotations in al-Shāfiʿī's *Umm*. Some variants alter only phrasing; others affect the degree of agreement a position claims, the narrator chain, or the teacher's attached explanation. Different recensions preserve variations in wording, attribution and juristic comment, so no single printed recension reproduces every form in which a teaching circulated. [El Shamsy, 2021](https://knowledge.uchicago.edu/records/a14wz-9hc46).

chapters.title: Legal schools emerge from the need to decide recurrent cases
chapters.book: Book V — How knowledge and spiritual formation acquired lasting institutions
chapters.matn: Merchants still sold on credit, spouses disputed entitlements, heirs divided estates and judges faced disagreements between neighbours. New places brought new customs and documentary practices, while transmitted guidance had to be applied to circumstances not described in identical terms by earlier reports. Teachers in Iraq, the Ḥijāz, Syria and Egypt developed methods for reaching and defending judgments. Abū Ḥanīfah's students preserved and extended Iraqi legal discussions; Mālik gathered reports and the practice of Madinan scholars; al-Shāfiʿī examined the authority of different kinds of proof; Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal became a prominent model of reliance on transmitted evidence. Over generations, their successors compared opinions, taught precedents and produced manuals. The resulting schools preserved characteristic procedures without freezing every judgment at the founder's death. They allowed communities far from the first centres to ask similar questions in a shared vocabulary, even while arriving at different rulings. Lawyers and judges thereby acquired influence independent of any single dynasty, although appointments, patronage and local social hierarchies continued to shape their work.
chapters.sharh:
Disputes over sales, agency and liability required jurists to apply transmitted rulings and broader principles to new transactions. Suppose a merchant gives goods to an agent who sells to a third party, then disputes the price or liability for loss. A jurist needs to know the contractual terms, local usage, rules of agency and the relation of evidence to general principle. Competing schools may differ because they classify the transaction differently, trust different reports or apply analogical reasoning under different restrictions. The legal concepts are formed precisely to make difficult cases teachable and repeatable. Al-Shāfiʿī's *al-Risālah*, Mālik's *Muwaṭṭaʾ*, writings transmitted from Muḥammad al-Shaybānī, and early Ḥanbalī collections should be read together with later school manuals, not treated as interchangeable finished codes.

The legal schools were historically made by students, teachers and later jurists. For this reason a school's 'position' in a late manual cannot simply be attributed to its eponymous founder. Theological commitments, juristic reasoning and actual courts intersected without being identical. The Sunni four-school map was also not a description of every Muslim juristic tradition: Imāmī and Zaydī law developed distinct authorities, and other early schools later lost institutional continuity. For broad historical interpretation use Wael Hallaq, *The Origins and Evolution of Islamic Law*; for the necessary critical note, compare its reconstructions with primary texts and other modern models of legal emergence. Jurists trained students to classify acts, resolve conflicts among reports and reason from principles when inherited formulations did not settle a new case.

A revealing manuscript-level comparison concerns Mālik's *Muwaṭṭaʾ*. Its transmitted recensions differ, and the version associated with Muḥammad al-Shaybānī sometimes sets Mālik's Medinan positions beside Ḥanafī objections. Teachers carried texts between cities, compared their variants and argued about the rulings attributed to earlier authorities. Later western recensions had their own histories of circulation and authority. A student who learns one line of argument about sales, inheritance or ritual practice may therefore enter a dialogue already shaped by several teachers. The school becomes a discipline when these arguments can be preserved, criticised and extended while remaining recognisably related. Wael Hallaq's histories of school formation provide a model for examining this institutional process, but individual recensions and their manuscript witnesses remain the primary controls.

One *Muwaṭṭaʾ* report describes Ibn ʿUmar sprinkling water in his eyes during *ghusl*, while recensions differ over Mālik's accompanying juristic judgment. One recension preserves the practice without Mālik's judgment; al-Shāfiʿī quotes Mālik's comment that it was not accepted practice, while two other recensions give comparable statements that it was not obligatory. The recensions distinguish Ibn ʿUmar's reported conduct, Mālik's interpretation of its legal force and the rulings attributed to later schools. Students and jurists used such variants to decide whether reported conduct established an obligation, a recommendation or a permitted practice. [El Shamsy's aligned references](https://knowledge.uchicago.edu/records/a14wz-9hc46), pp. 367–368.

chapters.title: Endowments, colleges and the social life of scholarship
chapters.book: Book V — How knowledge and spiritual formation acquired lasting institutions
chapters.matn: A teacher could attract students through learning and reputation, but lessons required rooms, books, food and sometimes long years free from earning a living. Rulers, merchants and wealthy families established endowed mosques, hostels and colleges to support teachers, students, Qurʾān readers, jurists and visitors. The Niẓāmiyyah founded in Baghdad in the eleventh century became a prominent example of organized patronage. Other towns developed institutions suited to local political and family arrangements. Endowments could secure a scholar's work beyond a patron's lifetime, yet appointments to teaching chairs also became prizes in contests among households and officials. Learning thus acquired durable places while remaining dependent on personal instruction and recognition. A student still needed a teacher who could explain difficult passages and authorize their transmission; a building did not automatically certify understanding. The college, household library, mosque and Sufi lodge therefore became connected, sometimes competing settings in which law, grammar, recitation, theology and spiritual conduct were taught.
chapters.sharh:
The institution of *waqf* connected property to an intended continuing purpose under legally defined conditions. Its resources could pay stipends, maintain lodging and support copying; they could also sustain the prestige of the founding household. Michael Chamberlain documents how medieval Damascene colleges operated through endowments, elite patronage, scholarly households and personal relationships rather than modern university bureaucracy. In Damascus, endowed institutions were bound to elite strategies, offices and ceremonies, while much learning still occurred personally and privately. George Makdisi's account of institutionalized education is an important comparison, not an uncontested template.

The Prophet's mosque accommodated worship and instruction; later endowed colleges financed teachers and lodging through arrangements developed under different political conditions. The Prophet's mosque sustained public worship and instruction; later cities with large populations required more differentiated means of financing teachers and accommodating traveling students. An endowment is a historical institutional solution, not an originally complete blueprint present in seventh-century Madinah. It can, however, be evaluated within the religious language of charity, useful knowledge and obligation to others. The college also exposes a tension between credential and formation: a person may acquire the right to occupy a chair through patronage without demonstrating wisdom, while an influential teacher may have no such office. Teachers cultivated *adab* and stable capacities through particular curricula, exercises, personal correction and habits of study, although their methods differed among institutions.

A student at an endowed college could receive a stipend, lodging and instruction tied to the founder's stipulations. The property yield might provide a regular stipend, which made years of study feasible; a founder's stipulations might also determine which legal school occupied the teaching position. A respected scholar might then receive students because of the office, because of established expertise or because both reinforced one another. Chamberlain's Damascus evidence is important because it permits those mechanisms to be separated. Endowments, appointments, scholarly households and personal teaching relationships shaped who could study and who obtained authority to teach. Teachers and students also disagreed over whether paid office and public prestige encouraged learning, competition or vanity. It cannot be answered by assuming every patron was either altruistic or self-interested.

chapters.title: Translation, theological controversy and the uses of reason
chapters.book: Book V — How knowledge and spiritual formation acquired lasting institutions
chapters.matn: Muslims confronted disagreements not only over actions but over what could be known about God, the world and human responsibility. Earlier debates about free choice, divine justice, attributes and the status of the Qurʾān developed among theologians who used argument to defend positions drawn from revelation and inherited instruction. Greek works on logic, natural philosophy and metaphysics became available in Arabic through translators working with Syriac and Greek learning. Thinkers such as al-Kindī and al-Fārābī fashioned new accounts of knowledge and its demonstration; physicians and mathematicians pursued different kinds of inquiry under the same broad literary language. Theologians and philosophers met on questions of causation, the soul and the beginning of the world, but did not necessarily mean the same thing by knowledge or proof. Al-Ashʿarī and al-Māturīdī emerged from different disputational settings and gave enduring Sunni theological vocabularies to these controversies. The encounter made the disciplines more technically precise while leaving unsettled which claims demonstration could establish and where revelation decisively guided judgment.
chapters.sharh:
Philosophers and theologians disputed whether created causes act with inviolable necessity and how such causation relates to miracles and divine agency. Different answers presuppose different accounts of nature, regularity and possibility. It would be a mistake to summarize all Ashʿarīs as holding a single identical philosophy of causation or to equate the whole of falsafah with denial of miracles. The problem is debated in al-Ghazālī's seventeenth discussion of the *Tahāfut*, but it had a longer prehistory in kalām and philosophical accounts of nature. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy's 'Occasionalism' entry gives a useful map of disagreement even about how to read al-Ghazālī's ultimate position.

Arguments about God's attributes, moral obligation and human action also arise from different sources. Early Muʿtazilī positions are not interchangeable, and Sunni Ashʿarī and Māturīdī schools later developed their own internal debates. Ibn Sīnā's distinction between essence and existence and his proof of the necessary existent entered many later theological treatises, despite strong criticism of other Avicennan doctrines. The crucial historical change is not that 'Greek reason defeated' or 'Islam rejected reason.' Methods of inquiry moved across disciplines, were adapted to particular problems, and became objects of criticism by new authors. Primary controls include al-Ashʿarī's *Maqālāt*, al-Māturīdī's *Kitāb al-Tawḥīd*, al-Fārābī's works on the sciences, Ibn Sīnā's *Shifāʾ* and al-Ghazālī's *Tahāfut*. Differences in authorship, date and formulation can change the meaning of a philosophical proposition and the objections later commentators raise against it.

The *miḥnah* offers an early case of theological language becoming an instrument of public authority. During the *miḥnah*, caliphal officials demanded declarations about the Qurʾān's createdness, making conformity to a theological position a condition of public service. Muʿtazilī theologians developed arguments about divine justice and unity beyond the court's coercive policies; later Sunni theologians also employed rigorous dialectical argument. Later Sunni theologians used intricate logical methods while rejecting the imposition of a doctrine by a caliph. The controversy involved distinct claims about divine speech, legitimate proof and the ruler's authority to enforce a doctrinal declaration. These are distinct but interacting processes.

chapters.title: Al-Ghazālī, al-Rāzī and the remaking of philosophical theology
chapters.book: Book V — How knowledge and spiritual formation acquired lasting institutions
chapters.matn: As knowledge became more specialized, the scholar who mastered one discipline could no longer assume that its methods answered every question. Al-Ghazālī studied legal reasoning, theological controversy and philosophy, then examined both the power and the limits of their claims. His later teaching joined the discipline of outward action to the examination of intention and character. Ibn Rushd, writing in al-Andalus, defended particular philosophical demonstrations against objections raised in al-Ghazālī's critique. In the eastern lands, Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī interrogated Ibn Sīnā's arguments about existence, definition, knowledge and the soul; Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Ṭūsī later answered and reorganized parts of that critical legacy. Their works entered new teaching chains through commentary and gloss, often in the same institutions that taught grammar, law and theology. A student could therefore meet rival accounts of the human intellect and causation within a shared curriculum of religious learning. Commentators preserved rival arguments, formulated objections and replies, and taught students to test the force of a demonstration rather than assume agreement.
chapters.sharh:
These are two interacting but distinct intellectual histories. In *Tahāfut al-falāsifah*, al-Ghazālī objects to identifiable claims associated with the philosophers, including an argument about causation and miracle; Ibn Rushd's *Tahāfut al-tahāfut* responds to the critique. The disagreement cannot be reconstructed adequately by the bare sentence 'reason and revelation were reconciled' or by assigning one universal causal theory to al-Ghazālī. His *Iḥyāʾ* is another undertaking, concerned with the ordering of worship, everyday action, destructive motives and saving virtues. Al-Ghazālī's critique of philosophical theses and his treatment of worship and character pursued related concerns within different genres and arguments.

A second history develops through the criticism of Ibn Sīnā's *al-Ishārāt*. Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī uses detailed commentary to expose problems in essence, existence, definition and demonstration; al-Ṭūsī's replies help establish a continuing debate. The *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy* entry on al-Rāzī documents particular positions and the care needed in inferring his considered conclusions from dialectical writings. This is a more exact account of the 'post-Avicennan' tradition than a list of names. Commentaries became intellectual instruments: by setting out a lemma, objection, response and further objection, they required students to inhabit the logic of a question before accepting a resolution. That is relevant to the larger history of formation because the discipline of judgment can be cultivated through argument as well as through repeated moral actions. The achievements and failures of those pedagogic practices must still be judged from actual texts and institutions, not an idealization of scholasticism.

The dispute over essence and existence turned on what definitions establish about things outside the mind. Ibn Sīnā argues that a thing's essence can be understood without thereby affirming its existence; al-Rāzī questions what such a distinction establishes about real beings and whether a definition yields knowledge of an external essence. The reply cannot be assessed by saying merely that the later thinker 'synthesized' theology and philosophy. The relevant lemmas and objections must be located, and different formulations of al-Rāzī's own position compared before selecting one. The later classroom practice of commenting line by line preserved these difficulties for students. It also introduced a risk of treating subtle distinctions as verbal contests detached from demonstration; whether that happened is a question about particular curricula and commentaries, not a verdict on late scholasticism as a whole.

chapters.title: The work of the heart becomes a teachable discipline
chapters.book: Book V — How knowledge and spiritual formation acquired lasting institutions
chapters.matn: A believer could fulfil an outward obligation and still struggle with vanity, anger, envy or attachment to reputation. The first generations had learned to examine intention through prayer, almsgiving, fasting, companionship and restraint. As Muslim communities grew, teachers gathered such questions into more systematic instruction. Al-Muḥāsibī asked how a person could recognize motives that concealed themselves from self-examination; al-Junayd was remembered for disciplined sobriety in spiritual life; al-Qushayrī preserved teachings, terms and biographical examples for later students. Al-Ghazālī arranged the ordinary life of worship, eating, work, marriage and fellowship alongside destructive and saving dispositions. Prayer, trade, speech, anger and hope all engaged the same person's intentions and character. Thus the concern for the inward life did not arise as a substitute for law or communal obligation. Teachers developed particular methods for addressing what correct outward action might leave unformed. Their techniques varied, and the later organized paths were still taking shape; what endured was the question of how knowledge and repeated action become a stable character.
chapters.sharh:
Al-Ghazālī's *Iḥyāʾ* supplies an unusually clear architecture of the question: devotional acts, habits of ordinary living, qualities that destroy and qualities that save. Qurʾān 91:7–10 concerns purification of the soul, 107:4–7 rebukes ostentatious worship, and the ḥadīth of intention relates actions to their purposes. A jurist might determine whether a required donation was validly made, while a teacher of the heart could ask whether the giver sought recognition and became hostile when unnoticed. They need not issue contradictory verdicts: validity, motive and character are different objects of examination. Al-Muḥāsibī's *al-Riʿāyah* pursues self-monitoring, and al-Qushayrī's *Risālah* records a vocabulary of states and stations. Al-Muḥāsibī, al-Qushayrī and al-Ghazālī developed different analyses of intention, spiritual states and disciplined conduct in their respective works.

The category of *malakah* can help explain the historical pedagogy, provided it is not attributed indiscriminately to the first Companions. Repeated action can establish ease and stability, but a habit formed through vanity is not the same thing as a virtue. The spiritual author therefore asks about knowledge, intention, repeated practice and the social circumstances that reinforce or undermine a disposition. This bridges the Sīrah's early concern with prayer and mutual obligation to later manuals without pretending that the manuals already existed in the Prophet's lifetime. Prayer, self-examination and companionship developed distinctive vocabularies as teachers addressed recurring problems of intention, action and conduct.

The practice of self-examination takes place under conditions that can foster or frustrate it. A wealthy person may have more opportunities to give but also more occasions for display; a judge may face a temptation to regard being right as proof of being virtuous; a scholar may confuse mastery of a text with self-knowledge. Al-Ghazālī's discussion of blameworthy traits becomes relevant to such people precisely because their ordinary roles carry moral risks. Al-Ghazālī treated prayer, trade, social duties and concealed motives as connected aspects of moral formation. Early warnings against vanity do not establish an unbroken institutional lineage to later Sufi lodges. The stronger connection is the persistence of concrete religious problems and documented practices through which teachers addressed them.

Al-Ghazālī's own preface to the *Iḥyāʾ* explains why he combines worship, ordinary dealings, destructive qualities and saving qualities: the visible action and the condition of the agent are complementary objects of *ʿilm al-muʿāmalah*. Thus a person's prayer, debt, household conduct and anger all become occasions for diagnosing the relation between knowledge, intention and action. Al-Qushayrī's discussion of *ikhlāṣ* distinguishes acting for other people's approval from admiring oneself for acting well; Ibn ʿAṭāʾ Allāh's aphorism gives concise form to the difference between the outward configuration of an act and its animating sincerity. Their terminology is later; their texts help explain why the history of religious practice generated disciplines of moral formation. [Iḥyāʾ introduction](https://ittiba.org/ota/kutuphane/tasavvuf-0505ghazali-ihyaculumdin-shamela0009472-ara1-completed); [Qushayrī on sincerity](https://islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1087/142/); [al-Ḥikam](https://usul.ai/ar/t/al-hikam-al-ataiyya).

chapters.title: From the teacher's company to enduring Sufi networks
chapters.book: Book V — How knowledge and spiritual formation acquired lasting institutions
chapters.matn: Students seeking spiritual instruction gathered around teachers whose conduct, teaching and prayers they trusted. Such relationships could remain informal, but travel, endowments and the movement of disciples gradually allowed them to outlast a single circle. By the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, residences and lodges supported instruction, hospitality, remembrance and service; later lineages developed recognizable methods and patterns of authorization. The Qādirī, Suhrawardī and Shādhilī traditions became influential through different regional paths, not by one centrally organized movement. In North Africa and Egypt, al-Mursī and Ibn ʿAṭāʾ Allāh transmitted the teaching of Abū al-Ḥasan al-Shādhilī; Ibn ʿAṭāʾ Allāh connected remembrance and reliance upon God with ordinary work. Ibn ʿArabī, writing in the same broad period, examined prophetic wisdom and the possibilities of human spiritual realization in a different metaphysical register. His interpreters, including al-Qūnawī and al-Farghānī, elaborated technical accounts of disclosure and Muhammadan perfection. These traditions overlapped in persons and settings without collapsing into one doctrine, and their spread depended upon teachers able to transmit both practices and ways of understanding them.
chapters.sharh:
Alexander Knysh, in *The New Cambridge History of Islam*, and Devin DeWeese's study of Sufi organizational patterns distinguish early ascetic circles from the diverse forms of *ṭarīqah* that acquired more durable organization from the twelfth century onward. Authority could descend through personal initiation, family succession or local custom, and a lodge might serve worship, hospitality, storage or public prestige. A lineage claim is a historical claim requiring examination; a devotional chain is not automatically a documentary record of uninterrupted administrative continuity.

The Shādhilī teachers addressed remembrance and reliance upon God in the circumstances of earning, family life and human relationships. Ibn ʿAṭāʾ Allāh's *al-Ḥikam* and *Laṭāʾif al-minan* do not simply prescribe withdrawal: they address the intentions and misconceptions of people who must act, earn and encounter others. They treated ordinary duties as occasions for testing intention, reliance and remembrance. Ibn ʿArabī's *Fuṣūṣ al-ḥikam*, by contrast, assigns distinctive wisdoms to prophets and asks about the relation between divine self-disclosure and human realization; Qūnawī and Farghānī develop this speculative vocabulary further. The Akbarian discussions of Muhammadan reality concern prophetic wisdom, metaphysical disclosure and spiritual realization, not merely commendable behaviour. Spiritual transmission had become a set of institutions and an intellectual tradition; their historical emergence and the truth of their metaphysical claims are distinguishable questions. Sufi teaching lineages developed historically through identifiable teachers, while Akbarian texts elaborated metaphysical accounts whose claims require separate philosophical argument.

A second distinction keeps the history accurate. Spiritual practices such as remembrance and self-accounting, the institutional form of a later *ṭarīqah*, and a metaphysical doctrine of *walāyah* are not interchangeable. Ibn ʿArabī discusses command, station and witnessing within a theory of realization; Qūnawī's *Miftāḥ al-ghayb* develops an ontological treatment of *wujūd*; Farghānī later systematizes the Muhammadan Reality in his commentary on Ibn al-Fāriḍ. The relevant sequence is a documented development of teaching and concepts, not evidence that every early community member used the later terms. [Hakim on *walāyah*](https://ibnarabisociety.org/the-way-of-walaya-souad-hakim/); [Chittick's translation of Qūnawī](https://ibnarabisociety.org/qunawi-on-the-one-wujud-william-chittick/); [SEP on Ibn ʿArabī](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/ibn-arabi/).

chapters.title: Cairo, Damascus and Jerusalem: government, learning and the Crusades
chapters.book: Book VI — An international civilization with many centres
chapters.matn: While scholars and spiritual teachers increasingly travelled across regions, political authority was divided among rulers whose territories and religious allegiances differed. The Fāṭimids founded Cairo in 969 and established Ismāʿīlī institutions of rule and learning beside the older centres of Iraq and Syria. Seljuk military rulers later entered Baghdad and governed extensive territories while acknowledging Abbasid caliphal prestige. Rival courts recruited soldiers, built hospitals and colleges, endowed mosques and sought scholarly support. In 1099 a crusading army captured Jerusalem, establishing Latin Christian principalities among Muslim and Eastern Christian populations. Recovery demanded more than an isolated battlefield victory. Nūr al-Dīn worked to consolidate Syria, while Ṣalāḥ al-Dīn took power in Egypt, ended the Fāṭimid caliphate there, and assembled forces able to recover Jerusalem in 1187. Trade, truces, pilgrimage and argument continued across the frontiers throughout the wars. The cities of Cairo and Damascus became important homes for jurists, scholars, craftsmen and Sufis, whose teaching relationships were not exhausted by the campaigns. The long conflict joined military resources, religious legitimacy and urban institutions without making the history of all those institutions reducible to crusading warfare.
chapters.sharh:
Muslim and Christian rulers fought, negotiated truces, exchanged envoys and traded with one another; neither population acted as one undifferentiated political bloc. The Latin principalities interacted with diverse eastern Christian communities and with Muslim dynasties that themselves fought rivals. Ṣalāḥ al-Dīn's military success depended on prior Syrian consolidation, control of Egypt's resources and treaties with local powers. The Arabic chronicles of Ibn al-Athīr, Ibn Shaddād's account of Ṣalāḥ al-Dīn and Latin narratives should be compared for events and motives. No single court chronicle is a transparent record of all participants.

This case also clarifies what an 'international Islamic society' meant. A traveler passing from Cairo to Damascus encountered different rulers but could find Arabic books, legal teachers, markets, hospitals and spiritual guides across the frontier. Political fragmentation sometimes increased patronage competition. Fāṭimid Ismāʿīlī institutions and Sunni endowments promoted different understandings of religious authority while sharing some urban and administrative forms. The coexistence of disagreement and common social practices needs explanation, not rhetorical celebration. Crusading warfare shaped taxation, fortification, migration and religious preaching; it did not create the scholarly networks from nothing. For orientation consult the *New Cambridge History of Islam*, volumes 2 and 3, and specialist biographies of Ṣalāḥ al-Dīn.

Al-Azhar's institutional history began in Fatimid Cairo and changed under subsequent governments and scholarly communities. Founded in Fatimid Cairo, the mosque became associated with a particular ruling dynasty's religious and educational project; its subsequent life passed through different political and doctrinal settings. It would be inaccurate to describe every later Egyptian scholarly institution as simply a continuation of Fatimid propaganda, yet a building's history can register changes in authority that a list of dynasties conceals. Similarly, military and charitable endowments under Nūr al-Dīn and Ṣalāḥ al-Dīn tied urban property to public aims, while actual teachers and students used those places in diverse ways. The wars shaped what cities could finance and whom they could protect. Endowed institutions financed teaching under differing patrons, just as individual campaigns depended on particular alliances, revenues and military aims.

chapters.title: Al-Andalus and the Maghrib: cities, scholarship and the loss of a political world
chapters.book: Book VI — An international civilization with many centres
chapters.matn: An Umayyad prince who escaped the Abbasid overthrow established a new ruling house at Córdoba in 756. Over generations al-Andalus became a western centre of Muslim government, agriculture, crafts and learning, connected across the Mediterranean to North Africa. Its rulers faced Christian kingdoms to the north and rival Muslim claimants within Iberia; its cities brought Arabic-speaking Muslims, Christians and Jews into relations of exchange, rivalry and unequal legal standing. Córdoba's caliphate later broke into competing city-based kingdoms, while the Almoravids and then Almohads connected parts of Iberia to powerful Maghribi states. Jurists carried Mālikī teaching across the straits; grammarians, physicians, philosophers and poets travelled between courts and scholarly circles. As northern Christian kingdoms expanded, Muslim authority contracted, leaving the Nasrid kingdom of Granada until its conquest in 1492. Muslims who remained in Christian-ruled territory encountered changing guarantees, pressures to convert and, ultimately, expulsion in the early seventeenth century. Books and teachers nevertheless crossed from Iberia into North Africa, and the intellectual history of the western Islamic lands continued after the loss of political rule. Scholars and merchants sustained learning and exchange across the western Mediterranean while warfare, restrictions on religious life and displacement changed the communities that produced them.
chapters.sharh:
The institutional trajectory is more informative than a rise-and-fall label. Umayyad rule in Córdoba was initially an emirate and only later a caliphate; the caliphal order ended in 1031, after which different *ṭawāʾif* competed for revenues, military support and legitimacy. Almoravid and Almohad movements emerged within North African conditions and intervened in Iberian politics, bringing their own doctrines and ruling practices. The Nasrid regime at Granada persisted for more than two centuries while balancing warfare, diplomacy, taxation and economic relations with its neighbours. María Viguera-Molins describes the collapse of the Cordoban caliphate in 1031 and the subsequent competing kingdoms, while archaeological studies document the continuing urban and agricultural life of al-Andalus.

Learning followed related but distinct pathways. The *Muwaṭṭaʾ* circulated in versions associated with western transmitters; Mālikī jurists acquired durable authority in the Maghrib and al-Andalus. Scholars could write Arabic commentaries and teach across the straits even when the regions were politically divided. Ibn Rushd's philosophical and legal writings belong to this western history, while Ibn ʿArabī's early life in al-Andalus and later movement eastward illustrates a transregional scholarly-spiritual trajectory. Neither philosopher should be used as a generic symbol of 'Andalusian openness': each must be read in their actual works and conditions.

Christian, Jewish and Muslim relations varied across cities, institutions and centuries. The concept *convivencia* is a subject of historiographical debate, not a license to erase coercion or shared daily life. The forced conversions imposed after Granada and the expulsion of Moriscos during 1609–14 are historically distinct from the conquest of 1492 itself. Communities and books displaced toward the Maghrib could survive political collapse, yet the material cost to families was severe. Archaeology, local documents, Muslim and Christian chronicles and the histories of particular scholarly households must be brought together before proposing a comprehensive interpretation of this region.

chapters.title: Persianate language, commerce and the circulation of books
chapters.book: Book VI — An international civilization with many centres
chapters.matn: Muslim societies had long shared Arabic as the language of revelation and many learned disciplines. Across Iran and Central Asia, Persian also became a vehicle for state correspondence, courtly writing, ethical instruction and poetry. Its influence travelled with administrators, poets, merchants and Sufi teachers into Anatolia and India. A student might read Arabic grammar and jurisprudence, learn Persian literary models and hear local languages at home. Courts cultivated prestige through histories and poetry, while traders carried goods and correspondence along roads joining Khurāsān, Baghdad, the Gulf and the Indian subcontinent. The use of paper, books and professional scribes allowed a work to outlive the place where it was composed. Yet transmission required readers who could interpret a technical term, patrons able to finance copying and teachers who corrected mistakes. The world of shared books and spiritual idioms therefore extended beyond any single sovereign's territory. Persianate culture did not replace Arabic learning; the two frequently occupied different but related roles in the education, administration and devotion of the same persons.
chapters.sharh:
Hodgson distinguishes Islam as a religion from the broader Islamicate culture of poetry, commerce and royal architecture; some authors nonetheless understood those cultural practices as means of religious realization. His categories themselves require qualification, especially where authors understood philosophy or poetry as an integral way of realizing religious truth. Shahab Ahmed argues that many Muslim authors understood philosophy, poetry and other Islamicate practices as integral to their religious lives.

Manuscript colophons, ownership records, citations and teaching certificates document particular routes by which texts passed among scholars. Niẓāmī's Persian narratives, Saʿdī's ethical works, or the legal and Sufi texts carried to South Asia are possible case studies, but their particular routes cannot be assumed from later popularity. Manuscript dates, ownership notes, colophons, reading certificates and library inventories provide stronger evidence. The intellectual consequence of bilingual learning also deserves attention: a technical Arabic discipline could be explained in Persian and eventually local vernaculars, changing who could enter a tradition without necessarily changing the tradition's formal terms. Such processes explain the civilization's adaptability more concretely than the phrase 'cultural synthesis.'

One route of inquiry is through the reconstruction of a book's movement. A Persian text copied at one court might reach India with a secretary, be read in a learned household and be cited in a later ethical manual. A documented textual route requires dated manuscripts, ownership notes, biographical notices or explicit citations; similar vocabulary alone does not establish transmission. Literary Persian also provided an intermediary language for local translations and commentaries. Students who learned Arabic legal terminology through Persian explanations could participate in a wider scholarly community while continuing to speak vernacular languages at home. Persian also mediated technical learning in administration, law and spiritual instruction among multilingual communities. It is about the practical mediation by which technical learning became teachable across regions without requiring every learner to begin with the same mother tongue.

chapters.title: Mongol conquest, conversion and the survival of scholarly worlds
chapters.book: Book VI — An international civilization with many centres
chapters.matn: In the thirteenth century Mongol armies destroyed cities, displaced populations and dismantled established regimes across Central and Western Asia. Baghdad was taken in 1258, ending the ruling Abbasid court there. Yet other Muslim centres survived, and new rulers needed scribes, merchants, physicians and administrators to govern the territories they had conquered. Mamluk armies stopped a Mongol force at ʿAyn Jālūt in 1260, while Cairo and Damascus continued to support judges, schools and the movement of books. In Iran, Mongol rulers first patronized several religious communities; Ghāzān's conversion to Islam in 1295 marked a major development in Ilkhanid political life. Rebuilding, new endowments and courtly histories followed among continuing wars and fiscal pressures. Older scholarly practices could thus be adopted by conquerors who had initially stood outside them. Teachers and merchants also moved along Mongol-controlled routes, even as warfare made many local livelihoods precarious. The loss of a capital did not extinguish Islamic learning, but the recovery of learning depended on surviving people, books, towns and resources, rather than on an abstract continuity immune to violence.
chapters.sharh:
The difference between a dynasty's conversion and a population's religious transformation is essential. Peter Jackson's *The Mongols and the Islamic World* and the *Encyclopaedia Iranica* account of the Mongols trace the varied trajectories of the Ilkhanids, Jochids and Central Asian khanates. Aḥmad Tegüder had already ruled as a Muslim Ilkhan; Ghāzān's accession later established a more durable public Islamic orientation at the court. Rashīd al-Dīn's histories should be read in the context of his court position, alongside Mamluk and other sources. Motives given to a conqueror by an official chronicler are evidence for political representation as much as for private conviction.

The mechanism of institutional persistence is visible in Cairo and Iran. A *waqf* could support a school across changes of dynasty, but endowments might be ruined or reallocated; a jurist's students could copy his work even when his patron was defeated. Mongol administrators also adopted Persian fiscal and literary practices for practical reasons. An Ibn Khaldūnian model can illuminate the transition from conqueror solidarity to the difficulties of administering settled societies, while local documents decide how far the analogy holds. After the Mongol wars, scholars continued to produce works in theology, logic, astronomy and Sufi thought, although warfare altered their centres, resources and patrons.

A later chronicler who says that Ghāzān's accession brought Islam to the Ilkhanate is reporting a major change in public royal identity, not the conversion of everyone under his rule. Aḥmad Tegüder and Muslim Mongol soldiers preceded Ghāzān's accession and therefore demonstrate earlier Islamic affiliations within Ilkhanid society. Later Mongol rulers' patronage of scholars, foundations and monuments also served political purposes, but religious conviction cannot be disproved merely by identifying those interests. The contrasting Mamluk and Ilkhanid reports should therefore be compared as partisan accounts of a contested transformation. Courts, colleges, manuscripts and commercial routes carried learned and devotional practices through changing dynastic conditions. Mongol campaigns devastated cities and scholarly households, while surviving people and institutions later rebuilt teaching and textual circulation under new rulers.

chapters.title: The Middle Niger: markets, kings and independent scholars
chapters.book: Book VI — An international civilization with many centres
chapters.matn: South of the Sahara, Muslim merchants had long crossed deserts to exchange salt, metals, textiles and other goods. Their routes linked North African towns with settlements and courts along the Niger. Rulers sometimes welcomed Muslim traders and employed literate specialists before most of their subjects adopted Islamic practices. Mali became a powerful kingdom, and Mansa Mūsā's pilgrimage in 1324 brought its wealth and connections to wider notice. Under later Songhay rulers, towns such as Timbuktu and Jenne supported jurists, merchants, teachers and book copying. Scholars acquired standing through knowledge, family networks and their ability to mediate disputes; some sought autonomy from rulers while relying on the same commercial communities for resources. Rural devotional life, local languages and courts did not always develop at the same pace. West African Muslim scholarship therefore emerged through local institutions and debates, not merely through the arrival of books from the north. Its authors participated in wider Mālikī and Sufi conversations while writing about the needs of their own societies.
chapters.sharh:
The *Tārīkh al-Sūdān*, learned biographies, manuscripts, archaeological evidence and reports by travellers such as Ibn Baṭṭūṭah preserve different aspects of the Middle Niger's history. Zachary Wright traces West African scholarly authority through teaching communities and inherited learned relationships, which did not depend wholly on appointment by royal courts. Northwestern University's West African Arabic manuscript collections and catalogues also make local textual production accessible.

Timbuktu supported learned families, libraries and teaching circles whose organization differed from modern universities; surviving manuscript inventories vary greatly in age and provenance. The age, provenance and content of particular libraries need separate examination. A study of 31 private libraries found variation in the age and provenance of collections, limiting claims of uninterrupted scholarly transmission across every household. The surviving libraries preserve evidence of local scholarship but differ in the periods and networks they document. Trade supported towns and literacy; rulers patronized institutions; scholars organized teaching and defended authority within those changing conditions. West African scholars used Arabic and Mālikī learning within local commercial, political and educational arrangements, adapting inherited disciplines to their own institutions.

Aḥmad Bābā (d. 1627), a West African scholar and author, offers a named route into this history. His works on Mālikī scholarship and learned biographies belong to a world that maintained ties with North Africa; his career was also affected by Moroccan intervention in Songhay and the removal of scholars from Timbuktu. Aḥmad Bābā's scholarly career and forced removal after Moroccan intervention connected the independence of learned households with struggles over political power.
